research.query: What is missing for the Moon?
research.answer:
The question was matched to: moon. Below is what the indexed documents state about it, quoted with their sources.

**Evidence**
- Atmosphere — Moon base / pressurized rover. 30.0–35.0 % O2, 54.0–70.3 kPa, lunar (planning_assumption). ACME CFI-G: 6 tests inside this envelope. [S10]
- DAFT / DAFT-2: Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter. DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. On the Moon, regolith dust will enter habitats: how will detectors discriminate dust from… [S1]
- CHALLENGE: No partial-gravity combustion data yet. PSI currently holds no combustion data at lunar or martian gravity. The challenge notes that microgravity and normal-gravity results can bound intermediate gravity levels, and that E-FIELD (PSI-22) mimicked partial gravity with… [S2]
- STDCE-1: Space Shuttle Missions: The culmination of the research effort involved conducting the STDCE experiments aboard the Space Shuttle, taking advantage of the extended microgravity environment to study thermocapillary flows over a broader range of parameters and conditions than… [S3]
- FLEX: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew… [S4]
- FLEX: These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. [S5]
- Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter: DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. Limitation: Terrestrial test dust, not lunar regolith; feasibility test only. [S11]
- BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations  [S12]

**Limits**
- Extractive answer (no language model configured): passages are quoted, not interpreted.
- Only documents in this knowledge base were searched.
warnings: Partial gravity: the PSI corpus holds microgravity and 1-g data only — values are bounds, not lunar or martian measurements.

sources.title: DAFT / DAFT-2 — Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2 — insight:daft-dust-vs-smoke
sources.text: Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter. DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. On the Moon, regolith dust will enter habitats: how will detectors discriminate dust from smoke to avoid nuisance alarms?

sources.title: CHALLENGE — insight:partial-gravity-gap
sources.text: No partial-gravity combustion data yet. PSI currently holds no combustion data at lunar or martian gravity. The challenge notes that microgravity and normal-gravity results can bound intermediate gravity levels, and that E-FIELD (PSI-22) mimicked partial gravity with ion-driven forces. For a Moon base, which results are bounding cases and which cannot be transferred at all?

sources.title: STDCE-1 — Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 — approach
sources.text: Space Shuttle Missions: The culmination of the research effort involved conducting the STDCE experiments aboard the Space Shuttle, taking advantage of the extended microgravity environment to study thermocapillary flows over a broader range of parameters and conditions than possible on Earth. This included meticulous execution of the test matrix, encompassing various heating modes, power levels, and free surface shapes, while collecting detailed flow visualization and temperature data.

sources.title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment — researchImpacts
sources.text: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft.

sources.text: These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.

sources.text: 2. Understanding soot formation aids in designing combustion systems with minimum emissions.

sources.title: BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids - II — researchImpacts
sources.text: A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you’re on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning.

sources.title: STDCE-1 — Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 — researchImpacts
sources.text: Materials Processing: The insights gained from STDCE have direct relevance to materials processing techniques on Earth, particularly those involving free surfaces and high-temperature gradients, such as welding, crystal growth, and the fabrication of thin films and coatings. Understanding and controlling thermocapillary flows in these processes can lead to improved product quality and reduced defect formation.

sources.title: ACME E-FIELD Flames — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames — researchImpacts
sources.text: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

sources.title: BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2
sources.text: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations are free text; flow units to be confirmed in the BASS-II documentation; flame-spread rates are in the raw video data.

sources.title: More oxygen: droplet flames more often survive to burnout
sources.text: FLEX droplet tests in N2-only atmospheres that ended in flame extinction before burnout — Heptane: 5/17 at 21 % O2 vs 0/11 at 30–34 % O2; Methanol: 9/12 at 21 % O2 vs 2/13 at 30–34 % O2. Remaining tests ended in burnout ('completion') or droplet disruption. Limitation: Isolated droplets, two fuels; 'extinction' here means the flame went out before the droplet was consumed (often radiative), not the action of an extinguisher. Counts, not a model.

sources.title: No partial-gravity combustion data yet
sources.text: PSI currently holds no combustion data at lunar or martian gravity. The challenge notes that microgravity and normal-gravity results can bound intermediate gravity levels, and that E-FIELD (PSI-22) mimicked partial gravity with ion-driven forces. Limitation: Bounding is not interpolation: behaviour at 1/6 g may not lie between the two cases for every metric.

top_passage.text: BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

top_passage.text: The Saffire-II experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions.
